category: anonymous temporary file host (pomf-style POST API)

free_tier.stated: Max upload size is 256MB. Expiry is chosen per upload from 1 day, 7 days or 30 days; no account and no email are asked for.
free_tier.notes: The offer is a per-object cap and a retention choice, not a byte allowance.

per_object_cap.notes: The page writes 256MB; the measured rejection point was not pushed to, so 256e6 is the page's decimal reading, not a measured byte boundary.

retention.stated: 1 day / 7 days / 30 days selected at upload. The default (no expiry field sent) produced expires=1795313693, which is 2026-11-22T02:14:53Z, exactly 30 days after the upload.
retention.notes: Measured from the epoch the API returned, not from the page.

egress.terms: Downloads are served from qu.ax itself; no byte allowance, no account and no published download counter. Nothing on the page meters traffic out.

interface_detail: POST https://qu.ax/upload.php as multipart/form-data, field name 'files[]'. The reply is JSON: files[0].url, .size, .hash (SHA-1), .expires (epoch seconds).
tooling: curl -F 'files[]=@file' https://qu.ax/upload.php; a ShareX .sxcu is published at /static/quax.sxcu
chaining: A 30-day, 256 MB anonymous mirror is the cheap middle tier of an archive: big enough for a single dataset shard, long enough to outlive a scrape job, and reachable by one curl line, so it composes with a scheduler and no credential store.

limits.value: 30 days maximum; the expiry is fixed at upload and cannot be extended
limits.source: measured: expires=1795313693 in the upload reply

limits_note: A file type allow-list runs before the size check: the same 1 MiB payload sent as payload-1mib.bin was refused with HTTP 400 {"message":"file type is not allowed","success":false}, and accepted once renamed to .txt. The download side is referer-gated: GET /x/leM7o.txt without a Referer answers 200 with an 8 254-byte HTML page, and the same request with Referer: https://qu.ax/leM7o answers 200 with the 1 048 576 bytes.
binding_note: At 1 TiB a month the 256 MB cap only means 4 000 uploads, which a loop handles; the hard stop is that nothing on the service extends a file past 30 days, so a re-fetch after a month needs the original bytes, which the client no longer has if this was the only copy.

identity_cost.detail: No account, no email, no cookie was sent; the upload was one POST from a bare HTTP client and a URL came back.

reliability_note: Two gates before the bytes: an extension allow-list refuses .bin outright, and the raw path /x/<id>.<ext> serves a 200 HTML landing page unless the request carries a Referer header from the file page. Both produce HTTP 200, so a client that trusts status alone reads an error page as a download.
confidence_note: Upload, read-back and digest all happened: 1 048 576 bytes posted, 1 048 576 bytes fetched from /x/leM7o.txt with the Referer header, SHA-256 matched. A push against the 256 MB edge would raise the cap from documented to measured.

evidence.proved: POST of 1 048 576 bytes as payload-1mib.bin -> HTTP 400 {'message':'file type is not allowed','success':false}; the same bytes as .txt -> HTTP 200 with files[0].url=https://qu.ax/leM7o and expires=1795313693 (2026-11-22T02:14:53Z)
the URL the API returned serves HTTP 200 with 8 254 bytes of text/html - the file page, not the file; its only download href is /x/leM7o.txt, which 302s back to the page when a Referer is absent

with 'Referer: https://qu.ax/leM7o' the same path returns 1 048 576 bytes of text/plain, sha256 da0099c231f1182a5d411c8ac5149dfb7a2e3578a3970928490cb78ba92aecc9, full-body hash matched the uploaded file
'Max upload size is 256MB' and the 1 day / 7 days / 30 days expiry choices

probe.download_requirements: Referer header; the API URL itself is a landing page

notes: The caveat is the extension allow-list, the 30-day ceiling and the referer-gated download. For a 20 TiB archive this is a distribution mirror, not storage: 80 000 files at 256 MB.
